title: Evanescent absorption spectroscopy of transition metal dichalcogenide materials using guided photoluminescence in Si$_3$N$_4$ photonic waveguides
authors: Victor Gonzalez-Morote, Marianna Sledzinska, Arkadiusz P. Gertych, Syed Hassan Abbas Jaffery, Mariusz Zdrojek, Daniel Navarro-Urrios
abstract: On-chip integration of two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with photonic waveguides underpins a growing class of compact optoelectronic and sensing devices, whose performance depends on the optical absorption of the 2D material in this integrated environment. We demonstrate source-free, on-chip evanescent absorption spectroscopy of MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$ flakes integrated on Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguides, in which the broadband defect-related photoluminescence of the Si$_3$N$_4$ core itself acts as the internal probe. Light generated inside the core propagates under the TMD flake and is spectrally attenuated by evanescent interaction with the 2D material, and normalizing the transmitted spectrum to a reference waveguide without TMD yields the energy-dependent absorption response without any external illumination. The extracted guided absorption agrees with Raman and local micro-photoluminescence characterization and resolves differences between spatially uniform and non-uniform flakes. A complementary top-pumping scheme recovers guided WS$_2$ photoluminescence, whose spectral reshaping during propagation is quantitatively reproduced by the measured absorption. This source-free platform qualifies 2D materials in their integrated photonic environment and provides a direct route toward waveguide-integrated TMD photodetectors and sensors.
summary: The paper introduces and validates a novel technique for measuring the optical absorption of 2D TMD materials integrated into $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ waveguides. By using the waveguide's own photoluminescence as an internal probe source, they achieve source-free, on-chip spectroscopy. This method directly quantifies how guided light interacts with the TMDs, providing critical data for developing next-generation integrated quantum optoelectronic devices.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a method to accurately measure the optical absorption of two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) while they are integrated into an operational photonic waveguide environment.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated source-free, on-chip evanescent absorption spectroscopy, showing that guided photoluminescence spectral reshaping quantitatively reflects the energy-dependent absorption response of the TMD layer.
method: They use the broadband defect-related photoluminescence generated within the $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ waveguide core as an internal light source, which then propagates and is attenuated by evanescent coupling with the overlying TMD flake.
model_or_system: The system involves transferring TMD flakes ($	ext{MoS}_2$, $	ext{WS}_2$) onto $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ photonic waveguides. Measurements compare this guided PL attenuation to local micro-photoluminescence ($\mu$-PL) and Raman characterization.
key_observables: Energy-dependent guided absorption spectrum ($	ext{dB cm}^{-1}$), spectral reshaping of photoluminescence, and comparison between uniform vs. non-uniform flake measurements.
important_parameters: Excitonic resonance energies (e.g., $\sim 1.83 	ext{ eV}$ for $	ext{MoS}_2$), coverage lengths ($L = 680 \mu	ext{m}$ to $1.2 	ext{ mm}$), and attenuation coefficients ($\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The technique assumes the PL generated in the core accurately represents the light interacting with the TMDs, and near resonance, reported losses are conservative lower-bound estimates due to saturation effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate sample sketches, comparison plots of transmitted vs. reference spectra, and detailed spectral measurements showing excitonic resonances and attenuation profiles for $	ext{MoS}_2$ and $	ext{WS}_2$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the necessity of in-situ characterization, details the source-free PL measurement technique using $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ waveguides, presents comparative results against local measurements ($\mu$-PL/Raman), and concludes by validating the platform for integrated optoelectronics.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful experimental tool for characterizing quantum material properties (excitonic absorption) under realistic device operating conditions, which is crucial input data for designing quantum photonic circuits or sensing elements.
